0: Companion practice pack: MiniCPM_ModelScope Purple Book_Chapters and Practice Pack_v0.1.zip
1: Author: Yang Zhizheng, Head of Developer Relations at OpenBMB Open Source Community, ModelScope Community Contributor
2: In the previous chapters, we have tried running models on computers and in the cloud.
3: However, for jotting down notes or looking up a piece of information in daily life, what we reach for more often is still our phone. Since open-source models can be downloaded, can we put one into a phone and let it directly handle some tasks for us on the phone?
4: Of course, a phone has limited memory, battery, and heat dissipation, so a model that runs on a computer may not run smoothly on a phone. Typically, we choose a smaller model, let it learn the requirements of a specific task, then reduce the resource footprint of its weights through quantization, and see how it actually performs on the phone.
5: This time, let's start with a small task like organizing to-dos. Jot down "work, submit project report at 18:00 on Friday, also need to water the plants", and we hope the model can extract the things to do separately, keeping the time when there is one and leaving it blank when not specified. If we later build a to-do app, such results would be convenient for the program to process further.
6: Around this scenario, we choose MiniCPM, complete a LoRA fine-tuning in ModelScope Notebook, then convert and quantize the model and run it on an Android phone.
7: Let's see what interesting things we can do on a phone.
8: 1. First define a small task suitable for a phone
9: In this chapter, we first complete the task of "extracting explicit and not-yet-completed to-dos from notes". The input is a piece of text, and the output is the following structure:
10: task uses the action phrase from the original text; due_text keeps the time description from the original text; category is filled only when the original text explicitly states "work, life, study, other", otherwise it is null. Multiple items are arranged in order of appearance; completed or canceled items are not included as to-dos; when there are no to-dos, return {"tasks":[]}.
11: Keeping the original time reduces a common error: the note contains "tomorrow", but the model does not know in which time zone and on what date this note was written. If we later integrate with a calendar, the app should carry the note time and time zone and separately complete time parsing and user confirmation.
12: After the task boundaries are determined, first test the base model with the same prompt. If it already meets your needs, you can still complete the experiment in this chapter to observe whether fine-tuning brings stability improvements.
13: 2. How a small MiniCPM model is trained
14: We use MiniCPM5-2B as the text model. It adopts the standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture, and the official releases include stage artifacts such as Base, Midtrain, SFT, and the final model, which makes it suitable for observing the relationships between training stages. In this chapter, we continue task fine-tuning on the final model, and the main model entry is OpenBMB/MiniCPM5-2B.
15: 2.1 Small models need to trade off between capability and running cost
16: A phone needs to reserve memory simultaneously for the operating system, various apps, model weights, KV cache, and temporary computation tensors. The purpose of choosing a small model is to complete a specified task under resource constraints. A small model does not mean that any task can be run easily; input complexity, output length, quantization precision, and the runtime engine all affect the final experience.
17: MiniCPM5-2B has a structure of 42 layers, 16 Query heads, and 2 KV heads, using GQA. Its total parameter count is 2,516,756,480, and its non-embedding parameter count is 1,981,982,720. "2B" is a scale label in the model name; when calculating the deployment footprint, the actual parameter count and files should be used. Estimating only the full weights at 2 bytes per parameter gives about 5.03 GB; this does not yet include runtime memory. This chapter starts with shorter inputs and shorter JSON outputs.
18: 2.2 What pretraining, mid-training, and post-training each solve
21: Role in the public MiniCPM5 training route
24: Build language and basic knowledge capabilities; the training route includes stable training and decay training
27: Strengthen capabilities such as code and math, and adapt to the target data distribution
29: Dialogue or task inputs and demonstration responses
30: Learn instruction following, response style, and specific task behaviors
33: Further optimize performance on tasks with evaluation signals
35: The teacher provides training signals for the student's generation behavior
36: Distill the capabilities of a specially trained teacher into the released model
37: The officially released UltraData series covers data directions such as web, code, math, SFT, and RL. For developers, what is worth learning is how data quality and training stages work together, rather than moving the entire training corpus into a single Notebook experiment. We only update a small number of LoRA parameters on the existing model.
38: 2.3 How LoRA enables the model to learn our task
39: LoRA freezes the base weights and adds trainable low-rank updates to specified linear layers. After a fine-tuning run, what you get is an adapter, which depends on the original base and cannot run independently as a complete model. To make it usable on a phone, this chapter will merge the adapter back into the base, then convert it to GGUF and quantize it.
40: The user in the data provides records, and the assistant provides JSON that conforms to the contract. Training learns how to process these inputs and how to produce outputs, not to add certain and reliable private knowledge to the model. In particular, rules such as "fill in null when there is no time" and "do not include completed items in the to-do list" need to be repeatedly reflected in the examples.

42: Download and extract the accompanying practice package, upload the entire minicpm-purplebook-draft directory in the ModelScope Notebook, and open notebooks/01_minicpm5_todo_lora.ipynb. This is a resource recommendation that leaves margin for first-time reproduction, and is not yet a measured minimum requirement. Ultimately, the actual Notebook image, GPU model, peak VRAM, disk usage, and training duration should be recorded. For selecting a runtime image and creating an instance, refer to Chapters 04 and 10 of the Purple Book; quotas and available resources are subject to what is displayed on the account at that time.

60: 3.3 Prepare training, validation, and test data
61: The companion package provides original synthetic instructional data: 320 training samples, 64 validation samples, and 96 test samples. The three sets use different peripheral phrasing templates, and the raw inputs are checked for duplicates. They include single-item, multi-item, cancellation, completed, no-todo, irrelevant time, and notes within records that require changing the output format.
62: The training file uses the messages JSONL supported by ms-swift, with one complete conversation per line:
63: The above example shortens the system prompt; the actual file contains the full prompt in examples/task_contract.py. Training, validation, testing, and mobile tasks should use the same contract.
64: Synthetic data is suitable for teaching readers to run through the pipeline. Although the expression templates are separated, the task vocabulary and generation rules are still shared, so it cannot prove that the model has adapted to all records of real users. Project acceptance should also supplement a real test set that is authorized, manually annotated, and not involved in parameter tuning. The validation set is used to adjust parameters and select checkpoints; the final test set is not used to select prompts or learning rates.
65: When hosting the dataset, publish the inputs, labels, splitting method, generation scripts, version, and license together to the ModelScope dataset repository. Before finalizing the main text, add the repository links actually created by both parties; the local files in the accompanying package can be used first for reproducing the draft.

89: 5. Compare base, fine-tuned, and quantized results
90: Test the base model first, then the merged weights, and finally the GGUF. Use the same test set, system prompt, output limit, and non-thinking mode for comparison. For ease of comparison, this experiment uses deterministic decoding; this is a task evaluation protocol, not a sampling recommendation for all MiniCPM inference scenarios.
91: The fine-tuned model must be merged first. Replace --adapters with the checkpoint path actually output by training; the example checkpoint-actual steps cannot be executed as-is:
92: The accompanying Notebook lists the actual checkpoints and allows selection, avoiding treating the example path as an already generated file.
99: Proportion of samples whose raw output can be parsed directly and whose fields and types satisfy the contract
103: Proportion of samples whose parsed result is exactly identical to the ground truth
106: Proportion of samples that correctly extract the number of items and whose output structure is valid
110: Compare the three fields in item order; both extra and missing items incur penalties
114: Proportion of fields whose reference answer should be null that still output null
117: Unparseable outputs, timeouts, and missing predictions are all counted as failures; before scoring, do not remove Markdown, do not repair JSON, and do not fill in fields. Field scoring for empty to-do samples is computed as one complete empty record, so they are not ignored in the statistics. All metrics should report both the sample count and failure examples.
118: EvalScope can use general_qa to organize this batch of test data and reports, with the entry point at examples/qa_evalscope.py. Its default BLEU and ROUGE are suitable for supplementary observation, but cannot determine "whether times are filled in out of thin air" or "whether cancelled items are treated as to-dos", so this chapter uses the task validation script as the primary basis. For general evaluation principles, continue reading Chapter 17 of the Purple Book.
119: Actual projects can also add a control of "base model plus a few example prompts" to determine whether the gains come from fine-tuning or prompt improvements. This group should be marked independently and must not be mixed into the main control with the same prompt.
121: GGUF is a model file format, and Q4_K_M and Q8_0 are quantization schemes. A trained LoRA adapter should first be merged into the full weights; the adapter must not be directly renamed to .gguf. MiniCPM5 is a text model and does not need mmproj.

143: 8. Run your own model on an Android phone
144: The main route uses the official OpenBMB MiniCPM-V Apps. Although the project name includes V, the public project also supports the MiniCPM5-1B and MiniCPM5-2B text models.
145: The model list of the official precompiled APK is fixed. This chapter uses source code to register your own GGUF, then builds and installs it. It is not a general import solution where "put the file into any directory and the official APK will recognize it." After registration is complete, the app's Model Manager can download your fixed-version model.
146: The script adds an entry to the model list in the official ModelInfo.kt, setting an independent model ID, ModelScope download URL, and file checksum; at the same time, it sets the same pending system prompt and non-thinking mode at the load and clear-session entry points of that custom model. A publicly downloadable repository is used here; private repositories require separately implementing authenticated downloads, and this chapter does not package account tokens into the mobile app.
147: Open vendor/MiniCPM-V-Apps/MiniCPM-V-demo-Android with Android Studio. The selected project declares NDK 27.0.12077973, CMake 4.1.2, and compile SDK 36.1. Install the matching components according to the actual Gradle prompts, and build in an environment with the SDK configured:
148: For the reader's hardware scope, first choose according to the official installation page's Android 8.0+, ARM64, and recommended at least 6 GB RAM; whether a specific phone can run it is subject to the actual test of the custom model in this chapter. The minimum API declared in the source code differs from the installation page; the main text adopts the more conservative scope of the installation page and does not promise compatibility for all devices based on it.
149: On the phone, select "My MiniCPM To-Do Assistant," complete the model download, and load it. The registration script will use the prompt in task_contract.py to generate TodoPrompts.kt, and call setSystemPrompt after that model is loaded and after the session is cleared. Clear the session before each test and keep non-thinking mode. The original chat interface does not have this task contract; if you skip the script and only paste the contract as a user message, that is a different prompt condition and the results should be marked separately.
150: After the download is complete, turn on airplane mode and enter a new record you have not seen before. Successful acceptance should simultaneously include: being able to generate a result that conforms to the contract, not calling a remote inference interface, and the model file coming from your own fine-tuned fixed version. Running the official original model can only verify the installation route and cannot replace verification of the custom artifact.
151: 9. Record phone experience and troubleshoot issues
156: Record model, system version, and available memory before loading
159: From clicking load to the model being able to receive input
161: From submission record to first output token
163: From submission to generation completion, including prompt processing
165: Number of generated tokens divided by actual decoding time, with tokenizer noted
167: Sample process memory with system tools, and record the sampling methodology
169: 20 consecutive entries with fixed input length, recording latency, failures, and heat
171: Enter new records and generate results in airplane mode
173: Do not treat character count as token count, and do not treat desktop GGUF service speed as phone speed. Report time to first token and full JSON completion time together to reflect the real interaction cost of the to-do assistant.
174: When model import fails, check file integrity, GGUF metadata, tokenizer, and engine commit; when thinking content appears, check the template and non-thinking settings; when memory is insufficient, reduce context and output limits and compare quantization schemes; when format degrades, locate data and contract issues from the original failure samples. When JSON is invalid, the app should retain the original text and allow regeneration or manual editing, and must not write erroneous results directly into the calendar.
175: The completion standard for this chapter is: your own ModelScope repository has traceable training and deployment artifacts, your own supported phone can load these artifacts, and new records can be converted into to-dos offline. At this point, fine-tuning, publishing, and on-device execution are connected into the same practice.
